## 2. Step 2 — the post's quotations (method and result)

Opened `process-lessons.md` at 02:05 IST (after §1 above). A script (scratchpad `quotes.py`, `tags.py`) extracted every string in quotation marks from the study (267), searched each in `page.txt` (curly quotes normalized; pieces split at "…"), and for every hit compared the post section it occurs in ([I] l. 1–16, [W] l. 17–29, [K] l. 30–56, [T] l. 57–71, [O] l. 72–82) with the next tag in the study's line. Result: every passage tagged [I]/[W]/[K]/[T]/[O] occurs verbatim in `page.txt`, in the tagged section. The only textual differences are conventional: nested double quotes rendered as single quotes (`'one unproven lemma.'`, `'good agreement.'`, `'footgun'`) and one bracketed edit of record text (`do[es]`). No misquotation of the post. The 141 non-hits are quotations of the record (Step 3) or single words. What the quotations get wrong is framing, not text: see F1 (P12 and §0 "one sentence"), F2 (§0 "What the post does not contain"), F9 (the P9 heading puts a phrase that is not the post's inside quotation marks), F10 (P8 dates a December experiment to "the first project"; P9 turns the post's "in almost all cases" into "every time").

**Amended texts.**

(u), amended: `STATUS.md` holds what a fresh session needs and nothing else: the protocol, the standing orders, ONE paragraph of current state, ONE queue, the task entries of the newest session, and a resume checklist that is true today. N" citation is read, and the closing LOG entry carries that commit and the hashes. The archive is read in windows, like the log, never whole. New citations name a standing order or a queue item by its number, never `STATUS.md` by line. (w), amended: A time stamp is produced by `scripts/stamp.py` — a placeholder filled in a brief or header, or a stamped line appended — and never typed; agents' briefs name the same script in place of `date`, and the script appends every stamp it emits to `rh-program/.stamps.log`. `stamp.py --check <the session's first commit>` runs at the close and before any squash or history rewrite; it flags a same-day entry or header stamp that is later than its commit or absent from `.stamps.log`; its output goes into the closing LOG entry, and a flagged stamp is corrected before the close. ## 8. Step 6 — what the study does not say

1. **A lesson of this very session, at the 10(p) threshold, not proposed.** The private e-mail of 2026-09-18 has now entered tracked files twice: the reply file itself was tracked verbatim until Session 41's purge removed "the verbatim private email (`c3-r/s14/correspondence/…-reply.md`)" from the history (`LOG.md` l. 2262), and tonight evidence reader D quoted two sentences of it because the brief "asked for a verbatim quote in every row" (`LOG.md` l. 2321). A kind in two units earns a warning line under 10(p). Proposed W-line (for the reconciliation, not a seventh rule): WRITER — "Private correspondence is paraphrased and cited by file and line, never quoted, even where a brief asks for verbatim quotes; the program's own summary lines may be quoted." READER — "Before a deliverable is committed, compare it with every file under `correspondence/` for shared runs of seven or more words (the check in section 4 of this read: a few lines of Python, positions only)." The study's §E.3(a) reports the slip's facts correctly but not its cause (a brief's quotation demand overriding a privacy rule) or that it is the second occurrence.
2. **The post's caution about automated checks, read only for plots.** "Even with all the monitors I set up, I've found the automated checks still can't be trusted" (`page.txt` l. 65) bears on a program in which every referee is an agent (ev. D Counts, "Human referees: 0") and 32 of 43 corrections came from a second model (ev. A). The study's P7 uses the sentence for pictures; §D(2) states the count; neither says that the post's author trusted his own eye over his monitors, while this program has only monitors and, by the study's own §0, no reader who owns the field.
3. **Further evidence for (u) and (w) that the study missed.** The Session-21 waste line records an Opus read's "truncated-line misreading" (`LOG.md` l. 1550) — the long lines of the record have already cost a read. `STATUS.md` l. 187 records a stamp written as "13:3x IST 2026-09-29" in Session 33 — a typed stamp with an unknown minute, a fifteenth session for F3's list.
4. **§E.3(a), the two slips of this session.** The stamp slip: accurately told (P4 and `ORCH-NOTES.md` N4 match `LOG.md` l. 2319 and the five AHEAD lines of `stamp.py --check`); the study does not count its own "three hours" (F16). The e-mail slip: facts accurate as of 02:00 (my 7-gram check confirms the current files clean); slightly loose — the deliverable held two sentences and `SHARED.md` one fragment (`LOG.md` l. 2321), the study says "two sentences … in old versions of two files"; overtaken at 02:14 (F11).
5. **§C refusals.** §C.1, 3, 6, 7, 8 hold. §C.2 conflates target and routes (F17). §C.4 is right, and rule (z) contradicts it (F15). §C.5 stands, on a premise stated too narrowly (F14).
6. **§D and §E.** §D(1) presents an unmeasured boot cost as a spend and policy handovers as its effect (F8); §D(2) undercounts the orchestrator's catches (F5); §D(3)'s "who else would care" is F15's judgment. §E.1 is accurate (`LOG.md` l. 2287; `STATUS.md` l. 26 S41 block; ev. C's timing note). §E.2 matches ev. B2 (b). §E.3(b) is accurate (ev. D Table 2 rows 3, 6, 7).
7. **A tension the study does not name.** Its P1 tally and the post's l. 8 both say the finished, checkable results come from known techniques on published objects; standing order 12(a) asks every session for a new mechanism. The study is right to leave the target to the sponsor (§C.8), and right that the two need not compete (P12); but a rule that nudges the funding mix — (z)'s published-object clause — is exactly where the tension would bite, which is why I would drop that clause (F12).
